vignette:
At seventy-two, Leonard had built a life of patterns and routines, yet beneath the surface, turmoil churned. A software engineer by trade, he often found solace in the logic of coding, where every line had a purpose and every function a clear outcome. But following the harrowing experiences of his past, his mind had become a prison itself. The trauma of being tortured during his time spent overseas had left scars deeper than the physical ones. In moments of solitude, he would recall the vivid details-the cold, stark room, the faces that twisted into menacing sneers, the unrelenting pain that seemed to seep into his very being. It was these memories, tightly interwoven with feelings of shame and despair, that gave rise to the belief that he had acted in ways that violated his core values. This internal conflict haunted him, leading him to monitor his thoughts obsessively, fearful that any slip might signify he was losing his grip on reality. His pervasive sense of being broken made him retreat from situations that could trigger those memories, reinforcing the belief that he was incapable of facing the world and further deepening his sense of unworthiness.

As Leonard navigated daily life, the world around him transformed into a landscape littered with potential threats. He had learned to scrutinize faces, dissecting every micro-expression and posture, convinced that danger lurked just beneath the surface. This vigilance seeped into his professional life as well; during team meetings, while others engaged in casual discussions, he remained on high alert, analyzing the body language of his colleagues for signs of deception or hostility. His belief that danger lurked just beneath the surface made it feel necessary to scrutinize every interaction, as he was convinced that failing to do so could lead to catastrophic consequences. When the threat felt this close, analyzing every detail of his colleagues' interactions was not merely a habit but a necessary strategy to feel somewhat secure in environments that otherwise felt unpredictable and dangerous. This constant sense of danger drove Leonard to adopt maladaptive strategies, such as scrutinizing his colleagues for signs of hostility, as a means to navigate a world he believed was fraught with risk. In that state of constant alertness, he found that checking the locks twice was the only thing that allowed his body to settle enough to sleep, as the perceived danger made it feel essential to take precautions against unseen threats. The need to stay vigilant extended into the quiet corners of his home, where he found himself checking locks and securing windows as if fortifying a fortress against unseen enemies. This perceived need for constant safety measures stemmed from his belief that the world was dangerous, leading him to adopt behaviors that he felt were essential for his survival. Sleep, which once provided a refuge, became elusive as he lay awake, trapped in a cycle of hyper-alertness, waiting for threats that never came. In that state of constant threat, he had found that checking the locks twice was the only thing that allowed his body to settle enough to sleep, a temporary relief that he felt he couldn't afford to forgo. This sense of imminent danger had led him to believe that he needed to take these precautions, as the thought of not doing so felt irresponsible in a world he perceived as fraught with risks. 

The constant threat he perceived around him only deepened his feelings of isolation. Leonard felt set apart from others, a specter haunting the edges of social gatherings, unable to connect. He had lost faith in people, convinced that trust was a vulnerability he could no longer afford. Leonard's decision to isolate himself was further reinforced by his maladaptive strategies; each time he avoided social interactions, he felt more convinced that he was different and unworthy of connection. This belief reinforced his decision to isolate himself, as each withdrawal from social situations served to confirm his view that he was fundamentally different and unable to handle the risks of connection. His negative appraisals had led Leonard to believe that avoiding social interactions was the only rational response to the perceived threat of rejection, reinforcing his conviction that he was too fragile to engage with others. Each time he chose to retreat into solitude rather than engage, he felt a deepening conviction that he lacked the resilience others possessed, reinforcing the belief that he was fundamentally unworthy of connection. Each act of avoidance further solidified his negative appraisals, as he interpreted his inability to cope with social interactions as evidence of his fragility, deepening the cycle of self-doubt that kept him isolated. Each time Leonard chose to retreat rather than engage, he felt a quiet confirmation of his negative beliefs, reinforcing the idea that he was not only different but fundamentally incapable of connecting with others. Friends had drifted away, their attempts to reach out met with Leonard's withdrawal, as he chose solitude over the risk of vulnerability. Each time he pushed someone away, he felt the weight of his isolation grow heavier, a tangible reminder of his belief that he was fundamentally different from those around him. 

In this cycle of negative appraisals, Leonard's thoughts bore the burden of regret and self-doubt. The more he monitored his thoughts for signs of insanity, the more he felt tethered to a sense of despair. He tried hard to suppress the memories of that dark time, believing that if he could just push the past out of his mind, he could reclaim some semblance of peace. Yet, each act of avoidance only deepened his conviction that he was broken, as he felt increasingly unable to cope with the very memories he sought to escape, reinforcing the belief that he was forever marked by his trauma. Each time he retreated from situations that could trigger those memories, he gathered evidence that he was incapable of facing the world, which only solidified his belief that he was fundamentally flawed. Yet in doing so, he only reinforced the belief that he was broken, reinforcing the very appraisals that kept him trapped. With every act of avoidance, he gathered evidence that he was not only unable to cope with his memories but also inherently flawed, deepening the cycle of self-doubt and despair. Every night spent awake in dread led him to a deeper conviction that he was forever marked by his trauma, forever unworthy of the connections he yearned for. 

It was a series of events that finally culminated in Leonard seeking help. After a recent incident where he felt overwhelmed by the need to check his locks repeatedly, he had realized that he could no longer navigate life alone. The fear of losing his grip on reality, of succumbing to the chaos within his mind, had become unbearable. He sat at his computer one evening, the glow of the screen illuminating his weary face, and he typed the words "help" into the search bar, hoping to find a way out of the darkness. What frightened him most was the prospect of opening up to someone, of sharing the pain he had bottled up for so long, but he knew that he could no longer live in isolation. With a heart heavy with trepidation, Leonard took the first step towards healing, hoping to reclaim the faith he had lost-not just in others, but in himself.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not establish that negative appraisals lead to maladaptive strategies, such as Leonard's compulsive checking behaviors.
  e.g. "If she had concluded that the world was dangerous and she was defenceless, staying home wasn't avoidance — it was the only rational thing to do."
  e.g. "The belief that speaking about it would make things worse kept her silent in her sessions, offering fragments instead of the whole picture."
  e.g. "Having decided that her feelings couldn't be trusted, she worked hard to stay numb — and had become quite good at it."
- Threat → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not indicate that perceived threat drives Leonard's maladaptive strategies, like hyper-vigilance and compulsive checking.
  e.g. "When the threat felt this close, planning her exit from every room she entered wasn't a symptom — it was just sensible."
  e.g. "She had found that checking the locks twice was the only thing that allowed her body to settle enough to sleep, so she checked them twice."
  e.g. "The only way to move through the world at that level of fear was to make it smaller — fewer places, fewer people, fewer chances for something to go wrong."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not convey that Leonard's maladaptive strategies reinforce his negative appraisals, such as the belief that he is broken.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."

vignette_attempts.vignette:
At seventy-two, Leonard had built a life of patterns and routines, yet beneath the surface, turmoil churned. A software engineer by trade, he often found solace in the logic of coding, where every line had a purpose and every function a clear outcome. But following the harrowing experiences of his past, his mind had become a prison itself. The trauma of being tortured during his time spent overseas had left scars deeper than the physical ones. In moments of solitude, he would recall the vivid details—the cold, stark room, the faces that twisted into menacing sneers, the unrelenting pain that seemed to seep into his very being. It was these memories, tightly interwoven with feelings of shame and despair, that gave rise to the belief that he had acted in ways that violated his core values. This internal conflict haunted him, leading him to monitor his thoughts obsessively, fearful that any slip might signify he was losing his grip on reality. His pervasive sense of being broken made him retreat from situations that could trigger those memories, reinforcing the belief that he was incapable of facing the world and further deepening his sense of unworthiness.

As Leonard navigated daily life, the world around him transformed into a landscape littered with potential threats. He had learned to scrutinize faces, dissecting every micro-expression and posture, convinced that danger lurked just beneath the surface. This vigilance seeped into his professional life as well; during team meetings, while others engaged in casual discussions, he remained on high alert, analyzing the body language of his colleagues for signs of deception or hostility. His belief that danger lurked just beneath the surface made it feel necessary to scrutinize every interaction, as he was convinced that failing to do so could lead to catastrophic consequences. When the threat felt this close, analyzing every detail of his colleagues’ interactions was not merely a habit but a necessary strategy to feel somewhat secure in environments that otherwise felt unpredictable and dangerous. In that state of constant alertness, he found that checking the locks twice was the only thing that allowed his body to settle enough to sleep, as the perceived danger made it feel essential to take precautions against unseen threats. The need to stay vigilant extended into the quiet corners of his home, where he found himself checking locks and securing windows as if fortifying a fortress against unseen enemies. This perceived need for constant safety measures stemmed from his belief that the world was dangerous, leading him to adopt behaviors that he felt were essential for his survival. Sleep, which once provided a refuge, became elusive as he lay awake, trapped in a cycle of hyper-alertness, waiting for threats that never came. In that state of constant threat, he had found that checking the locks twice was the only thing that allowed his body to settle enough to sleep, a temporary relief that he felt he couldn't afford to forgo. This sense of imminent danger had led him to believe that he needed to take these precautions, as the thought of not doing so felt irresponsible in a world he perceived as fraught with risks. 

The constant threat he perceived around him only deepened his feelings of isolation. Leonard felt set apart from others, a specter haunting the edges of social gatherings, unable to connect. He had lost faith in people, convinced that trust was a vulnerability he could no longer afford. Leonard's decision to isolate himself was further reinforced by his maladaptive strategies; each time he avoided social interactions, he felt more convinced that he was different and unworthy of connection. This belief reinforced his decision to isolate himself, as each withdrawal from social situations served to confirm his view that he was fundamentally different and unable to handle the risks of connection. Each time he chose to retreat into solitude rather than engage, he felt a deepening conviction that he lacked the resilience others possessed, reinforcing the belief that he was fundamentally unworthy of connection. Each act of avoidance further solidified his negative appraisals, as he interpreted his inability to cope with social interactions as evidence of his fragility, deepening the cycle of self-doubt that kept him isolated. Friends had drifted away, their attempts to reach out met with Leonard's withdrawal, as he chose solitude over the risk of vulnerability. Each time he pushed someone away, he felt the weight of his isolation grow heavier, a tangible reminder of his belief that he was fundamentally different from those around him. 

In this cycle of negative appraisals, Leonard's thoughts bore the burden of regret and self-doubt. The more he monitored his thoughts for signs of insanity, the more he felt tethered to a sense of despair. He tried hard to suppress the memories of that dark time, believing that if he could just push the past out of his mind, he could reclaim some semblance of peace. Yet, each act of avoidance only deepened his conviction that he was broken, as he felt increasingly unable to cope with the very memories he sought to escape, reinforcing the belief that he was forever marked by his trauma. Each time he retreated from situations that could trigger those memories, he gathered evidence that he was incapable of facing the world, which only solidified his belief that he was fundamentally flawed. Yet in doing so, he only reinforced the belief that he was broken, reinforcing the very appraisals that kept him trapped. With every act of avoidance, he gathered evidence that he was not only unable to cope with his memories but also inherently flawed, deepening the cycle of self-doubt and despair. Every night spent awake in dread led him to a deeper conviction that he was forever marked by his trauma, forever unworthy of the connections he yearned for. 

It was a series of events that finally culminated in Leonard seeking help. After a recent incident where he felt overwhelmed by the need to check his locks repeatedly, he had realized that he could no longer navigate life alone. The fear of losing his grip on reality, of succumbing to the chaos within his mind, had become unbearable. He sat at his computer one evening, the glow of the screen illuminating his weary face, and he typed the words "help" into the search bar, hoping to find a way out of the darkness. What frightened him most was the prospect of opening up to someone, of sharing the pain he had bottled up for so long, but he knew that he could no longer live in isolation. With a heart heavy with trepidation, Leonard took the first step towards healing, hoping to reclaim the faith he had lost—not just in others, but in himself.
